summary: Defines MIB textual conventions for the Facility and Severity values commonly used in syslog messages, so other MIB modules can reuse them instead of defining their own. This is a Proposed Standard.

eli5.summary: This gives standard names to labels such as where a message came from and how serious it is, so every program uses the same names.

questions: what is a textual convention in a mib
subtitle: Standard names and numbers for syslog Facility and Severity, ready for reuse in MIB modules.

tldr.problem: Many MIB modules that deal with syslog messages would otherwise each define their own way to represent the Facility and Severity of a message.
tldr.mechanism: This MIB module defines two textual conventions, SyslogFacility and SyslogSeverity, that map labels to the numeric codes used in syslog messages.
tldr.outcome: Other MIB modules can import these conventions, and the mapping MUST be used in a MIB network management interface.

today: RFC 5427 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the textual conventions that other MIB modules can import for syslog Facility and Severity.

sections.title: Background
sections.content:
Operating systems, processes and applications, collectively called Facilities, generate messages about their status or events. These are known as syslog messages. A message generally carries a code for the Facility that generated it and a code for its Severity, and both are commonly used to categorize and select received messages.

Facility codes do not always identify the originator precisely. Implementations of the syslog protocol (RFC 5424) that contain structured data elements (SDEs) should use them to clarify the originating entity. This document defines textual conventions (TCs) for Facility and Severity codes.
sections.eli5: Programs write notes about what they are doing. Each note says who wrote it and how important it is, and this memo gives those labels standard names.

sections.title: The Management Framework
sections.content: Managed objects live in a virtual information store called the Management Information Base (MIB), generally accessed through SNMP. Objects are defined using the Structure of Management Information (SMI). This memo specifies a MIB module compliant with SMIv2, described in RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580. The overview of the framework is in section 7 of RFC 3410.
sections.eli5: Network gear keeps its facts in a big shared notebook with strict rules about how entries are written. This memo follows those rules.

sections.title: SyslogFacility
sections.content:
The SyslogFacility convention is an integer enumeration of 24 Facilities, numbered 0 to 23, for example kern (0), user (1), mail (2), daemon (3) and local0 (16) through local7 (23). For interoperability and backwards compatibility, the mapping between label and number is normative, and it MUST be used in a MIB network management interface even if a syslog implementation uses a different mapping elsewhere.

The labels are often semantically weak. There is, for example, no Facility label for an HTTP service, which might log as local7 or uucp. The labels for codes 4, 10, 13 and 14, and the code for the label cron, are known to vary across operating systems. To tell codes 9 and 15 apart, code 15 is labelled cron2.
sections.eli5: There is a numbered list of 24 senders, like a class roll call. Some systems call a few of them by different names, so the memo says which name goes with which number.

sections.title: SyslogSeverity
sections.content:
The SyslogSeverity convention enumerates eight levels, from emerg (0) to debug (7). Like Facilities, the label-to-number mapping is normative for interoperability.

The RFC notes that the label is often semantically meaningless, because the criteria syslog originators use for each level are implementation-dependent and have historically been so. An application might log messages as crit on subjective criteria, and operators can still configure syslog to forward them.
sections.eli5: Severity is a scale from "everything is on fire" to "just chatting". The memo gives each step a number and a name.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The module defines no management objects, only conventions that other MIB modules may use, so the RFC says it has no impact on the security of the Internet. Users of these conventions should read the security considerations of RFC 5424, since objects built with them may introduce security issues.

IANA recorded syslogTCMIB as { mib-2 173 } in the SMI Numbers registry.
sections.eli5: This memo only makes labels, not anything that can be attacked. Whoever uses the labels has to think about safety in their own work.
